answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for a cluster/account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (for Cosmos DB / DocumentDB accounts).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in Azure CLI group az cosmosdb (core CLI). Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource of type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts'. Terraform (azurerm provider): resource 'azurerm_cosmosdb_account'.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical Mongo-compatible connection string for the managed DocumentDB service: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@<account>@. For SRV: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb. Port for the non-SRV endpoint: 10255 (TLS).

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is typically billed as a managed compute tier (vCore-style machine sizes for Mongo clusters; examples use M-series tiers such as M30) plus storage and I/O; not per-request-unit (RU) like Cosmos SQL. Expect per-vCore (or tier) + storage billing rather than RU billing for the Mongo/DocumentDB clusters.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary auth is MongoDB username/password (SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-256). The service also supports Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) integration for token-based auth: obtain an AAD access token for the database resource and provide it to the driver as the credential (driver configured with authMechanism and the token as the password). Common usage in Node.js: acquire an AAD access token via @azure/identity, then connect with the mongodb driver using authMechanism=PLAIN or the recommended AAD-specific mechanism and the token as the secret in the connection string.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB client libraries for your language (e.g. official Node.js driver 'mongodb' or Mongoose). There is no special DocumentDB runtime client library for application data plane; Azure SDKs are only for management/ARM operations.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Supported vector index types (in this cluster) include DiskANN, HNSW and IVF. Example Mongo-like index creation (approximate form you would run in the mongo shell): db.carts.createIndex( { embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vectorIndexType: 'HNSW', dimensions: 768, metric: 'cosine', efConstruction: 200, M: 48 } ).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text/hybrid search is done by integrating the cluster with a search service (Azure Cognitive Search) or by using the service's built-in vector + text search features when available. Practically: either push documents into Azure Cognitive Search (indexer or pipeline) or use the provider's native vector+text search operators (a specialized text+vector query stage provided by the DocumentDB-managed Mongo layer).

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cluster supports MongoDB server/wire protocol version 7.0 (and recent 6.x compatibility). Common unsupported or partially supported features: server-side JavaScript ($where), some admin commands that require native MongoDB internals, and occasionally advanced server-side modules/commands that depend on a native MongoDB server implementation. Expect most CRUD, aggregation, and driver features to work but verify features like change streams, server-side JS and certain system collections.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no official local emulator that fully matches the managed DocumentDB Mongo API. For local development run the official MongoDB Docker image (e.g. mongo:7) on port 27017: docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo mongo:7. Use the standard mongo driver pointed at mongodb://localhost:27017 for tests.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams are supported only when the cluster exposes a replica-set/oplog interface; some managed clusters require enabling an oplog or a specific cluster tier to get change stream support. If supported, use the standard MongoDB changeStream APIs; otherwise plan to use polling or push events through an external change-capture pipeline. Check the cluster's replica/replica-set settings and enable oplog if required.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: The service is covered by the 'documentdb' MCP server (service-specific MCP server). Use the documentdb MCP server's default profile to obtain data-plane inspection and index tools. The general Azure MCP server does not provide the service-specific inspection capabilities for DocumentDB clusters.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft used the name 'DocumentDB' for the precursor NoSQL service which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. The modern managed Mongo-compatible offering is commonly referred to as DocumentDB or Cosmos DB's Mongo API in Azure documentation; it is not the same as any unrelated open-source 'DocumentDB' project. In short: Azure DocumentDB historically became Cosmos DB; the Mongo-compatible service is a Mongo-wire-protocol-compatible layer provided by Azure's managed service.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath is the service's managed Mongo-compatible engine (a Cosmos DB/DocumentDB implementation of the MongoDB wire protocol or an Azure-managed Mongo-compatible cluster), not necessarily a vanilla MongoDB server binary. Application code should use the standard MongoDB drivers unchanged for normal operations, but beware of server-side differences (unsupported admin commands, behavioral differences for indexing/transactions, and any provider-specific index or vector features).

answers.question: Which database in the cluster should the sample use?
answers.answer: Use database name sample_retail_12 for all collections and operations the sample creates.

answers.question: How should the sample read the cluster connection string at runtime?
answers.answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI; do not hard-code credentials. Example in Node.js: const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI;

answers.question: What collection and index does the sample need for abandoned-cart queries?
answers.answer: Collection: carts. Indexes: an index on lastUpdated (ascending) to find carts older than 2 hours: db.carts.createIndex({ lastUpdated: 1 }); and an index on customer.contactPreference for filtering. If embeddings are stored for copy-generation, create a vector index on embedding: db.carts.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vectorIndexType: 'HNSW', dimensions: 768, metric: 'cosine' }).

answers.question: What Node.js client and connection options should the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the official mongodb driver (npm install mongodb). Connect with a TLS-enabled connection string and options: const client = new MongoClient(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { tls: true, retryWrites: false, replicaSet: 'globaldb', useNewUrlParser: true, serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 10000 });

answers.question: How will the sample log results back to the cluster after orchestration?
answers.answer: Write an outcomes collection (sample_retail_12.orchestration_logs) and insert one document per cart processed with fields: cartId, processedAt, agentResults (copy text, channel), deliveryStatus, and error. Use standard insertOne/updateOne operations from the Node.js mongodb driver.
